evidence.craft: Read model.py, run.py, figure.py, tests/test_model.py, pyproject.toml, README.md. Small, readable numpy with docstrings stating units; sensible structure (crossing/noise_only/handheld as functions). Defects: the inconsistent zero clamp between merge() and the plain-mean arms (model.py:95 vs run.py:128); large_psnr hard-codes read noise 3.0 and renders each scene twice (run.py:131-132), so changing handheld's read argument would silently compare against a 3 e- large frame; estimate_shift wraps the refined peak with `> m/2` after refinement, fine; Fourier shift is periodic and the 6 px crop covers the 2 px wrap. Acceptable research code.
evidence.claims: Every numeric claim in README.md and research/README.md:810 traces to results.txt and recomputes (see checks). Disclaimers present: 'Produced with AI assistance', 'Everything here is synthetic', a long and honest Limitations list including that the 40 dB cap is this resampler's property (README.md:39) and that no confidence intervals are reported. Novelty is stated modestly ('elementary algebra'). Weaker: the headline (README.md:3) states 'registration blur adds frames in bright light (about 21 for A = 4)' as a finding although the body shows it is an artefact of the chosen resampler; the equal-read-noise-per-pixel assumption, which is what makes the dark limit A^2, is not called out as an assumption. Live page loaded (200).
evidence.fitness: A researcher building on burst-vs-sensor-size could reuse the harness (procedural scenes, Poisson-Gaussian capture, crossing interpolation), and the follow-up research/sensing-burstcap already does. But the result is not new: the A (shot-limited) to A^2 (read-limited) break-even is the CCD SNR equation applied to frame stacking (Howell, Handbook of CCD Astronomy, 2nd ed. 2006, ch. 4; the sub-exposure read-noise penalty is standard in astronomical stacking), and Hasinoff, Kutulakos, Durand & Freeman (ICCV 2009, 'Time-constrained photography') and Hasinoff, Durand & Freeman (CVPR 2010, 'Noise-optimal capture for high dynamic range photography') derive the same read-noise cost of splitting an exposure and the optimal bracket; neither is cited. Synthetic only, no real raw bursts. Sound as a pedagogical check, below a publishable increment.
evidence.domain: Against standard practice (Foi et al. 2008 noise model; Hasinoff 2010 merge weights; HDR+ 2016 merge): the noise model and the variance algebra are right, and the fixed-total-exposure framing (section C) is the comparison a sensor scientist would ask for. Departures: (1) the merge's per-frame clamp max(e, 0) is a biased estimator in the read-noise-limited regime and is applied to some arms only; (2) the bracket merge weights frames by exposure (sum e / s sum t), which is ML for pure Poisson but not the inverse-variance weighting Hasinoff 2010 shows is optimal once read noise is present; (3) equal per-pixel read noise for a pixel of A times the area is assumed silently (real large-pixel sensors differ in conversion gain and read noise); (4) PSNR only, no CIs. Disclosed limits (no ghosting, no robust merge, synthetic) are honest.

defects.what: merge() clamps every frame at zero (np.maximum(e, 0)) while the unregistered arm and the large frame are plain unclamped means, so section D compares a biased estimator against unbiased ones. At P = 30 the clamp alone is worth +2.7 dB (known-shift merge 18.70 clamped vs 15.98 unclamped; unregistered 15.71; large 16.83), which is why even the 'failed alignment' (3.1 px RMS) estimated merge beats the large frame; +0.5 dB at P = 100 (feeds D2's N* 5.9/6.8); nil at P >= 300. Headline numbers unaffected. Repro: /usr/bin/python3.13 /tmp/claude-0/audit-sensingburst/scripts/clamp.py.

Five of seven seeded mutants survive the 12 tests: removing the merge clamp, dropping the N read-noise term in var_burst_fixed_time (changes every section C ratio), gamma 1/2.2 -> 1, the clip threshold 0.98 fw -> 0.5 fw, and the sign of the sub-pixel peak refinement. The merge test uses zero read noise; nothing in run.py is tested.

Nearest prior work not cited and novelty not positioned: the A (shot-limited) to A^2 (read-limited) break-even is the CCD SNR equation applied to stacking (Howell 2006), and Hasinoff et al. ICCV 2009 ('Time-constrained photography') and Hasinoff, Durand & Freeman CVPR 2010 ('Noise-optimal capture for HDR photography') derive the read-noise cost of splitting exposures and the optimal bracket. Only HDR+ (2016) and Foi (2008) are cited.

Headline states 'registration blur adds frames in bright light (about 21 for A = 4)' as a finding, but it is an artefact of the chosen Fourier resampler (noise-free check: 42.5 dB cap for quarter-pixel shifts, none for integer shifts), as README.md:39 itself says; the research index repeats it unqualified.

Equal per-pixel read noise for a pixel of A times the area is assumed but not listed as an assumption; it alone produces the A^2 dark limit. Bracket merge uses exposure-proportional (Poisson ML) weights rather than inverse-variance weights once read noise is present (Hasinoff 2010).
large_psnr hard-codes read noise 3.0 and re-renders each scene twice, so changing handheld()'s read argument would silently compare against a 3 e- large frame.
run.py docstring says 'a few minutes on one CPU core'; it runs in 21 s (README's ~30 s is right).

verdict: A small, honest, reproducible synthetic study: results.txt reproduces byte-for-byte, and every headline number I recomputed independently holds (break-even algebra, 2M-draw Monte Carlo, fixed-exposure ratios, simulated N* within seed noise, the resampling cap's cause, the HDR bracket). It misses the bar on verification (5 of 7 seeded mutants survive) and sits at 2 on fitness and domain: the central A-to-A^2 result is the textbook stacking SNR equation and Hasinoff 2009/2010 is not cited, and the merge's per-frame zero clamp makes the low-light hand-shake rows (P = 30, 100) a biased-vs-unbiased comparison worth up to 2.7 dB. Finished (completeness 3), not at senior-professional level as research.
